🔔 Can DATA Network bring lasting activity to Sui? 

📣 DATA Network plans to retire its independent chain and run its AI training data registry on Sui, with Walrus handling files. Sui Foundation is investing $30 million in the network. A registry that its backers say already records millions of receipts daily could bring activity to Sui; how much of that translates into recurring SUI demand remains an open question.

⭐️ Sui Foundation’s October 12 announcement  says Trace, a rights registry for AI training data, is joining its stack. Walrus will store encrypted original files and Sui will record programmable rights and settlements. DATA Network’s own chain will eventually close. The foundation says its $30 million commitment makes it the largest institutional holder of the DATA Network, alongside PIP Labs and the DATA Foundation. The statement does not publish a completed migration date or a dollar amount of fees the business expects to pay on Sui. 

⚠️ Trace registers a data contribution, its origin and the rights attached to it. The foundation says the system has processed more than 250 million contributions since a June launch and averages over 3 million receipts a day. Applications named in the announcement include Kled, Numo and Oto. Kled is described as an opt in human data marketplace with more than 1.5 billion records being onboarded. Those are participant supplied operational claims; the release does not contain an independently audited breakdown by customer, chain, fee or paying AI lab. 

🔖 DATA Foundation says Trace settles payments to contributors when their data is licensed. A nurse’s consented account, a dashcam clip or a factory worker’s demonstration might be recorded as training material with use rights. The registry entry is not necessarily the complete source file. Its design separates a claim about who supplied data and who may use it from storage of the bytes. Sui and Walrus are meant to handle those parts after migration.

📌 Gorgan, IRNA – Brigadier General Yadollah Javani, deputy for political affairs of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), underscoring the full combat readiness of the Iranian Armed Forces to counter potential threats, says any miscalculation by the enemy will prompt a crushing response.

Speaking at the Administrative Council of the northern province of Golestan on Wednesday, General Javani addressed the regional and global consequences of the US-Israeli aggression, stating that the war imposed on Iran is not labeled a world war, but global public opinion considers it one.
​
He explained that the US-Israeli war on Iran had the same nature and characteristics as World Wars I and II, which impacted the global order, the geometry of power, and the shifting power equation—creating new realities.
​
The Iranian nation, the Resistance Front, and the Muslim countries of the region would witness the Islamic Republic emerging victorious, he emphasized, adding that the reason US President Donald Trump is reluctant to accept defeat is his anxiety over the domestic repercussions of the Iranian nation's victory.
​
Elaborating on US calculations before the start of the "Ramadan War" in February, he said the enemies were under the impression that, through the new aggression—specifically the sinister plot involving the martyrdom of the Leader of the Islamic Revolution—they could achieve their objectives in days, but in vain.
​
Pointing to the Leader's assessment before the war, General Javani said the same perspective was held by Imam Khomeini—that "America can't do a damn thing against us"—and the view held by Martyr Soleimani—that 'if you start the war, we will dictate its end'—were present in this conflict as well.
​
The IRGC official noted that even American politicians had acknowledged that Trump held no more military trump cards against Iran, whereas Iran still possesses such advantages. Any mischief by the enemy will prompt Iran's crushing and decisive responses, he added.
​
Referring to Iran's evolving capabilities, he said new technologies, weaponry, and equipment have bolstered the country's defense—a reason the US was forced to move its aircraft carriers some 700 to 800 kilometers away. "Today, the Persian Gulf region—which previously hosted over 100 military vessels and warships—is free of foreign military forces."
​
General Javani further noted that the enemy might once again commit a miscalculation; however, Iran has moved past the danger of a surprise invasion and is now well-prepared to respond to the enemy and counter any potential errors on its part.
​
On US economic pressure, he said the enemy had calculated that it might be possible to pressure Iran through a naval blockade, yet such an option is not feasible given the country's geography, its neighbors, and existing interconnections and interdependencies.
​
"Soon, the world will acknowledge that neither a naval blockade can bring Iran to its knees, nor are air or land blockades viable options," he said, adding that the enemy resorted to such measures after failing in its imposed war, psychological operations, and cognitive warfare.
